div.p: In Ephesus there lived a man among the foremost in power there, Lycomedes by name. To this Lycomedes was born, by a local woman named Themisto, a son, Habrocomes, a great marvel of beauty such as had never appeared before, either in Ionia or in any other land.

So Euxinus and Corymbus stayed together, waiting to hear what reply they would get, and they hoped to win the pair over easily. But Habrocomes and Anthia came to the little room where they usually stayed, and when they had told one another what they had heard, they threw themselves down and wept and lamented.

So that day they returned to the cave, and what little strength they had left they restored to themselves and to their horses; for Hippothous too had a horse hidden in the wood. The next day they passed by Cilicia and made their way toward Mazacus, a great and beautiful city of Cappadocia.

So Habrocomes was being led to Alexandria to stand trial for having, as it was thought, killed his master Araxus; meanwhile Hippothous and his men set out from Tarsus and went on the road toward Syria, making subject to themselves everything they met. They burned villages and slaughtered many men. And so, going on, they came to Laodicea in Syria, and there stayed, no longer as robbers, but as men who had come to view the city.

So Anthia was shut up in the pit with the dogs, and Amphinomus each time comforted her and made the dogs gentle by feeding them. Habrocomes, completing the voyage from Egypt, did not reach Italy itself (for the wind drove the ship off and turned it from the direct course), but brought it to Sicily, and they put in at Syracuse, a great and beautiful city.

This Habrocomes grew daily more beautiful, and along with his bodily graces the goods of his soul flowered together with them. He cultivated every branch of learning and practised music of many kinds; hunting, riding, and fighting in armour were his accustomed exercises.

"O father," they said, "O mother, O dearest fatherland, and household, and kinsmen!" At last Habrocomes recovered himself and said, "O ill-fated that we are, what shall we suffer in a barbarian land, given over to the outrages of pirates? The prophecies are beginning; already the god is exacting from me the penalty for my pride. Corymbus is in love with me, and Euxinus with you.

For from there Hippothous planned, by gathering young men in their prime, to form a robber band again. As they went through large villages there was abundance of all provisions, for Hippothous was skilled in the Cappadocian tongue, and everyone treated him as one of their own.

There Hippothous made inquiries whether he might somewhere find Habrocomes; but as he accomplished nothing, they recovered themselves and turned toward Phoenicia, and from there toward Egypt; for they had decided to overrun Egypt.

When Habrocomes came there, he decided to go about the island and search whether he might learn anything about Anthia. So he lodged near the sea with an old man named Aegialeus, a fisherman by trade. This Aegialeus was poor and a stranger, and made a bare living from his trade; but he received Habrocomes gladly, regarded him as his own son, and loved him beyond measure.

He was an object of devoted attention not only to all the Ephesians but also to the inhabitants of the rest of Asia, and they placed great hopes in him, that he would be a citizen of distinction. They treated the youth as a god, and there were already some who, on seeing him, bowed down and offered prayers.

O for the beauty that is so ill-timed in the eyes of both of them! Was it for this, then, that I was kept chaste until now—to submit myself to a robber in love with a shameful desire? And what life is left to me, becoming a whore instead of a man, robbed of my own Anthia?
Completing the journey in ten days, they came to Mazacus, and there settled near the gates and decided to recover themselves for some days from their toil.

Having gathered a great band, they went on the road toward Pelusium, and sailing on the river Nile to Hermoupolis in Egypt and to Schedia, they entered the channel of the river made by Menelaus; they passed by Alexandria, came to Memphis, the holy city of Isis, and from there to Mendes.
And at last, from their long companionship, Habrocomes told him his story, and spoke of Anthia and his love and his wandering; and Aegialeus began the story of his own life.

The youth thought highly of himself, and prided himself on the achievements of his soul, but far more on the beauty of his body. He looked down on everything else that was called beautiful as inferior, and nothing seemed to him worthy of Habrocomes, no sight, no sound.
But no—by the chastity that has been my companion from boyhood until this very hour, I will never submit myself to Corymbus; I will die first, and be found a corpse that is chaste."
And as they were feasting, Hippothous groaned and shed tears; Habrocomes asked him the cause of his tears. He said, "My story is a long one, and full of tragedy."

They took with them some of the local people as partners in the band and as guides for the road. Passing through these places, they came to the city of Leontopolis, and after passing through not a few other villages, most of them obscure, they came to Coptos, near Ethiopia.
"I," he said, "child Habrocomes, am neither a Sicilian nor a native of this place, but a Spartan, a Lacedaemonian, of those who are foremost in power there, and I had great abundance.

If he heard that some boy was handsome or some girl shapely, he laughed at those who said so, as not knowing that he alone was beautiful. Love he did not even consider to be a god, but cast him out altogether, accounting him as nothing, saying that no one would ever fall in love or submit to the god against his will.

So he spoke, and wept; and Anthia said, "Alas for our troubles! Already we are being driven to break one of our oaths, already we taste slavery. Someone is in love with me, and hoped to win me over and come to my bed after Habrocomes, and lie beside me and satisfy his desire.
Habrocomes begged him to tell it, promising to relate his own as well. So, taking it up from the beginning (for they happened to be alone), Hippothous told his story.

There they decided to rob, for there was a great throng of merchants passing through, of those who travelled to Ethiopia and to India; and their band numbered five hundred men. Seizing the heights of Ethiopia, and arranging everything, they decided to rob those who passed.

When I was young I fell in love with a girl, a fellow citizen, Thelxinoe by name, and Thelxinoe loved me in return. When an all-night festival was being held in the city, we came together, the god guiding us both, and we enjoyed what we had come together for.

If anywhere he saw a temple or a statue of Love, he laughed, and declared himself more beautiful than any Love. And so it was: for wherever Habrocomes was seen, no statue appeared beautiful and no painted image won praise.
But may I never become so fond of life, nor endure to look upon the sun after being outraged. Let this be resolved: let us die, Habrocomes; we shall have each other after death, troubled by no one."

For some time we were together in secret, and we swore to each other often to love until death; but some god grew jealous of us. While I was still among the youths, Thelxinoe's parents gave her in marriage to a young man of the country, Androcles by name; and Androcles was already in love with her.

At first the girl made many pretexts to put off the marriage; but at last, finding herself able to be with me, she agreed to leave Lacedaemon by night with me. So we dressed ourselves as young men, and I cut Thelxinoe's hair short.

On the very night of the wedding, then, we left the city and went to Argos and Corinth, and from there set sail and came to Sicily. The Lacedaemonians, learning of our flight, condemned us to death. But we lived here in want of provisions, yet glad, and thinking that we enjoyed everything, because we were together.
And here, not long ago, Thelxinoe died, and her body is not buried; for I keep it with me, and always love her and am with her."

As he spoke he led Habrocomes into an inner room and showed him Thelxinoe, a woman old now, but to Aegialeus still as beautiful as a girl; her body had been embalmed in the Egyptian manner, for the old man was skilled in this too.

"To her, then, child Habrocomes," he said, "I always talk as to one living, and lie beside her and feast with her; and if ever I come back weary from fishing, the sight of her consoles me. For she does not appear to me such as she now seems to you; but I think, child, of what she was in Lacedaemon, and what she was in our flight. I think of the festival nights, I think of our compact."

While Aegialeus was still speaking, Habrocomes lamented and said, "But you, most unhappy girl of all, when shall I find you again, even dead? To Aegialeus the body of Thelxinoe is a great comfort of his life, and now I have truly learned that true love has no limit of age.

But I wander over every land and sea, and have not been able to hear anything of you. O unhappy oracles! O Apollo, who gave us the cruellest of all prophecies, take pity now and give the fulfilment of what you foretold."

At this Love grew angry, for the god is contentious and pitiless toward the proud. He sought some stratagem against the youth, who seemed hard for the god himself to capture. So he armed himself fully, took up all the power of his amorous charms, and marched against Habrocomes.

This is what they had resolved. Meanwhile Apsyrtus, the chief of the brigands, learning that Corymbus and his men had come and were bringing many marvellous goods, came to the estate. He saw Habrocomes and his company, was struck by their beauty, and at once, thinking it a great profit, asked for them.

"I am," he said, "by birth from the city of Perinthus (the city is near Thrace), of those who are foremost in power there; and you have heard how famous Perinthus is, and how prosperous the men there.

When Habrocomes came before the governor of Egypt (for the people of Pelusium had reported to him what had happened, and the murder of Araxus, and that, being a slave, he had dared such things), the governor, learning each thing, and without even inquiring into what had happened, ordered Habrocomes to be led off and fastened to a cross.

So Habrocomes, lamenting thus and comforted by Aegialeus, lived in Syracuse, now sharing too in Aegialeus' trade. Meanwhile Hippothous and his men had built up a great band, and decided to leave Ethiopia and undertake greater enterprises.

A local festival of Artemis was being celebrated, with a procession from the city to the temple, which is seven stades away. All the local maidens had to walk in procession richly adorned, and the young men of the same age as Habrocomes. He himself was about sixteen years old, was enrolled among the youths, and held the foremost place in the procession.

The rest of the goods and possessions and all the captured maidens he distributed to Corymbus and his men; but Euxinus and Corymbus, though unwilling, gave up Habrocomes and Anthia to Apsyrtus—gave them up, in fact, under compulsion.

While I was young I fell in love with a beautiful youth; the youth was one of the local people, and his name was Hyperanthes. I fell in love first when I saw him wrestling in the gymnasium, and I could not hold out.

He was dumbstruck by his troubles, but consoled himself for his death by the thought that Anthia too seemed to have died. Those to whom this had been assigned led him to the banks of the Nile; there was a sheer cliff looking out over the stream of the river.

For it no longer seemed to Hippothous enough to rob man by man, unless he also attacked villages and cities. So, taking those with him and loading up everything (he had many beasts of burden and not a few camels), he left Ethiopia and went toward Egypt and Alexandria, and planned to make for Phoenicia and Syria again.

A great crowd had gathered for the spectacle, many of them townspeople and many strangers, for it was the custom at that festival for bridegrooms to be found for the maidens and wives for the young men.
So they departed; and Apsyrtus, taking Habrocomes and Anthia and two servants, Leucon and Rhode, led them to Tyre.
So when a local festival was being held, and an all-night vigil at it, I went up to Hyperanthes and begged him to take pity on me. The youth heard me and, taking pity, promised everything.

They set up the cross and fastened him to it, binding his hands and feet with cords; for this is the manner of crucifixion among the people there. Then they left him and went away, supposing that the one fastened up would remain secure.

He supposed Anthia to be dead. But Amphinomus, who guarded her in the pit, being amorously disposed and unwilling to be parted from the girl through his tenderness toward her and the calamity that lay upon her, did not follow Hippothous, but slipped away unnoticed among the many others and hid himself in a cave with the provisions he had gathered.

The members of the procession passed by in file: first the sacred objects, torches, baskets, and incense; after these horses, dogs, and hunting gear, some of it for war but most for peace. And each of the maidens was adorned as if for a lover.

Their procession was a spectacle for all to see, and everyone marvelled at their beauty; and the barbarians, having never before seen such loveliness, thought that those they beheld were gods, and counted Apsyrtus blessed for the kind of slaves he had acquired.

The first stages of love were paved with kisses and touches and many tears from me; at last, finding our opportunity, we managed to be alone together, and our age put us above suspicion. And for a long time we were together, loving each other beyond measure, until some divinity grew jealous of us.

But he, looking up at the sun and seeing the stream of the Nile, said, "Most kindly of the gods, you who hold Egypt, through whom both land and sea have been revealed to all men: if I, Habrocomes, am guilty of any wrong, may I perish miserably and undergo a still greater punishment, if any greater there be;
When night came, Hippothous and his men had come to a village of Egypt called Areia, wishing to plunder it; but Amphinomus dug open the pit, brought out Anthia, and urged her to take heart.

At the head of the line of maidens was Anthia, daughter of Megamedes and Euippe, of the local people. The beauty of Anthia was a thing to marvel at, and she far surpassed the other maidens. She was fourteen years old, her body was in the flower of its loveliness,
Leading them into his house, he handed them over to a trusty servant, ordering him to keep them with all care, since he expected to make a great profit if he sold them at their proper price.
There came from Byzantium (and Byzantium is near Perinthus) a man among the foremost in power there, proud of his wealth and abundance; he was called Aristomachus.

but if I have been betrayed by a wicked woman, may the stream of the Nile never be defiled by the body of one who perishes unjustly, and may you never look upon such a sight, a man who has done no wrong perishing upon your soil."

And when she was still afraid and suspicious, he swore by the sun and the gods of Egypt that he would indeed keep her pure of marriage, until she herself should one day be persuaded and willing to consent. Anthia trusted Amphinomus' oaths and followed him; and the dogs did not leave them, but, having grown familiar, were fond of them.

and the elegance of her bearing added much to her grace. Her hair was golden, mostly let loose, a little of it braided, and it stirred with the movement of the breezes; her eyes were lively, bright as a young girl's, yet stern as a chaste woman's; her tunic was deep purple, belted to the knee, falling to the elbows, a fawnskin wrapped about her, a quiver slung from her shoulder, a bow and javelins carried, and dogs following.

As soon as he set foot in Perinthus, as if sent by some god against me, he saw Hyperanthes with me and was at once captivated, marvelling at the beauty of the youth—beauty that could draw anyone whatever.

So he prayed, and the god took pity on him: a gust of wind arose suddenly and fell upon the cross, and washed away the earth of the cliff in which the cross had been fixed; Habrocomes fell into the stream and was carried along, neither harmed by the water, nor hindered by his bonds, nor injured by the beasts, but borne onward by the stream.
So they came to Coptos, and there decided to pass the days until Hippothous and his men should be far along the road; and they tended the dogs, that these might have provisions.

Often when they saw her at the precinct the Ephesians bowed down to her as to Artemis. And so on this occasion too, when she appeared, the crowd cried out, and the voices of the onlookers were of many kinds: some, in their astonishment, said she was the goddess; others, that she was someone else fashioned by the goddess in her likeness. But all prayed and bowed down and called her parents blessed; and Anthia the beautiful was on the lips of all who beheld her.

Having fallen in love, he no longer kept his passion within bounds, but at first sent messages to the youth; and when that was impossible for him (for Hyperanthes, out of his affection for me, would let no one approach), he persuaded the youth's father, a base man and weaker than money.
Carried along, he came to the mouths of the Nile, and there the guards took him and led him, as a fugitive from punishment, to the man who governed Egypt.

Hippothous and his men, falling upon the village of Areia, killed many of the inhabitants and burned the houses; and they went down not by the same road but by way of the Nile. For gathering all the boats from the villages between, they embarked and sailed toward Schedia, and . . . and from there, disembarking, they made their way along the banks of the Nile through the rest of Egypt.

When the throng of maidens had passed by, no one spoke of anything but Anthia. But when Habrocomes appeared with the young men, then, though the spectacle of the maidens had been a fine one, everyone who saw Habrocomes forgot them and turned their gaze upon him, crying out, struck by the sight, "Beautiful Habrocomes!" and "such as no other, the very image of a beautiful god."
His father gave him Hyperanthes on the pretext of teaching, for Aristomachus claimed to be a master of rhetoric. Taking him, he at first kept him shut up, and after this departed for Byzantium.

The governor, angrier still and thinking him wholly wicked, ordered them to make a pyre, lay Habrocomes on it, and burn him. Everything was made ready, and the pyre was beside the mouths of the Nile, and Habrocomes had been laid on it, and the fire set beneath; but just as the flame was about to touch his body, he prayed again briefly, as best he could, that the god would save him from the present evils.

Some even added this: "What a marriage it would be between Habrocomes and Anthia!" And these were the first exercises of Love's art. Soon the report about each of them reached the other: Anthia longed to see Habrocomes, and Habrocomes, until then untouched by love, longed to see Anthia.

I followed too, despising all my own affairs, and I was with the youth as much as I could be; but I could do little, and a kiss became a rare thing for me, and talk difficult, for I was watched by many.

And thereupon the Nile swelled into waves, the stream fell upon the pyre, and quenched the flame. What had happened was a marvel to those present, and taking Habrocomes they led him to the governor of Egypt, told him what had occurred, and related the help of the Nile.

At last, no longer able to bear it, I goaded myself and went back to Perinthus, sold all the property I had, gathered the money, and came to Byzantium; and taking a small sword (this too seemed good to Hyperanthes), I went by night into the house of Aristomachus, found him lying with the boy, and, filled with rage, struck Aristomachus a mortal blow.
The governor marvelled to hear what had happened, and ordered him to be kept in prison, but to be given every care, "until," he said, "we learn who the man is, and why the gods care for him so."

While all was quiet and everyone at rest, I went out unnoticed, just as I was, taking Hyperanthes with me; and travelling all night to Perinthus, I at once boarded a ship, with no one knowing, and sailed for Asia.

For a while the voyage went prosperously; but at last, when we were off Lesbos, a violent wind fell upon us and overturned the ship. I swam along with Hyperanthes, supporting him and making his swimming lighter; but when night came the youth could endure no longer, gave out in the swimming, and died.

I managed only to bring his body safe to land and to bury it. With many tears and groans, I gathered his remains, and finding somewhere a suitable stone, I set up a pillar over the tomb and inscribed on it, in memory of the unhappy youth, an epigram that I composed on the spot:

Hippothous made this tomb for renowned Hyperanthes, no fitting grave from death for a holy citizen, deep beneath the earth—a glorious flower, whom once a divinity snatched away on the sea, while a great gale blew.

After that I resolved not to go to Perinthus, but turned through Asia toward Greater Phrygia and Pamphylia; and there, from want of a living and from despondency at my misfortune, I gave myself to a robber band. At first I became a servant of the band, but at last I myself organized a band around Cilicia, which was renowned for a long time, until my companions were taken not long before I saw you.
Such is the fortune of my story. But you, dearest, tell me your own; for it is clear that you too are under some great compulsion in your wandering."

So when the procession was over, and the whole crowd had gone into the temple to sacrifice, and the order of the procession had broken up, men and women, young men and maidens came together to the same place. There they saw one another, and Anthia was captured by Habrocomes, while Habrocomes was overcome by Love. He kept gazing more and more steadily at the girl, and though he wished to tear himself from the sight he could not, for the god pressed hard upon him and held him fast.

Such was the state of Habrocomes and his company. A few days later Apsyrtus went off on another trading venture to Syria; and his daughter, Manto by name, fell in love with Habrocomes. She was beautiful, of an age now ripe for marriage, but far inferior to the beauty of Anthia.

So Habrocomes told that he was an Ephesian, that he had fallen in love with a girl and married her, and of the oracles, and the journey abroad, and the pirates, and Apsyrtus, and Manto, and the bonds, and the flight, and the goatherd, and the road as far as Cilicia.

So Habrocomes was in prison. But Psammis, who had bought Anthia, decided to return home and made all preparations for the journey; he had to travel through Upper Egypt to reach Ethiopia, where the band of Hippothous was.

Meanwhile the governor of Egypt had learned of what had happened at Areia, and of Hippothous' band, and that they were coming from Ethiopia. So he made ready many soldiers, set over them as commander one of his own kinsmen, Polyidus, a young man graceful to look upon and noble in action, and sent him against the robbers.

Anthia too was in a sorry state, receiving with her eyes wide open the beauty of Habrocomes as it streamed into her, and now scorning what is fitting for maidens. She would say something so that Habrocomes might hear, and would bare what parts of her body she could, so that Habrocomes might see. He surrendered himself to the sight and was the captive of the god.

This Manto, from her daily association with Habrocomes, was captured by love, and was beside herself, at a loss what to do. She did not dare speak to Habrocomes, knowing that he had a wife and never hoping to win him over, nor to any of her own people, for fear of her father.

While he was still speaking, Hippothous joined him in lamenting and said, "O my parents, O fatherland that I shall never see again, O Hyperanthes, dearest of all to me! You, Habrocomes, will at least see your beloved and recover her at last in time; but I can never see Hyperanthes again."
Everything was ready—many camels and donkeys and baggage horses; there was a great quantity of gold, much silver, and much clothing; and he took Anthia along too.

This Polyidus, taking the army, met Hippothous and his men at Pelusium, and at once, beside the banks, there was a battle, and many fell on each side; but when night came on, the robbers were routed, and all were slain by the soldiers, though some were also taken alive.

And then, when they had sacrificed, they departed in grief, blaming the swiftness of their parting; and wishing to look at one another, they kept turning round and lingering, and found many pretexts for delay.

For these reasons she was the more inflamed and in a sorry state. No longer able to bear it, she decided to confide her love to Rhode, Anthia's foster-companion, who was of the same age, a young girl; for she hoped that she alone would help her toward her desire.
As he spoke he showed a lock of hair and wept over it. When both had lamented their fill, Hippothous, looking at Habrocomes, said, "There is another story I passed over without telling.

When she, having passed Alexandria, came to Memphis, she prayed to Isis, standing before the temple: "O greatest of the gods, until now I remain pure, accounted yours, and I keep my marriage to Habrocomes undefiled; but from here I am going to the Indians, far from the land of the Ephesians, far from the remains of Habrocomes.

Hippothous alone, throwing away his arms, fled by night and came to Alexandria; and from there, managing to escape unnoticed, he boarded a ship that was putting out and set sail. His whole impulse was toward Sicily; for there he thought he would best escape notice and find a living, and he heard that the island was great and prosperous.

But when each had gone home, then they realized into what evils they had fallen. The memory of the other's face came over them, and love was kindled within them, and through the rest of the day they fed their desire; and when they went to sleep they came all at once into their distress, and the love within each of them was beyond all checking.

So, finding a moment of leisure, she led the girl to the household shrine of her father's gods, begged her not to betray her, took oaths from her, told her of her love for Habrocomes, implored her to help, and promised much if she would.

A little before the band was taken, a beautiful girl came wandering to the cave, of the same age as you, and she said your fatherland was hers; more than that I did not learn. It was decided to sacrifice her to Ares. Everything was made ready, when our pursuers came upon us; and I escaped, but what became of her I do not know.

So either save me, ill-fated as I am, from here, and restore me to Habrocomes while he lives; or, if it is wholly fated that we die apart from one another, grant me this, to remain chaste to the dead man."

"Know," she said, "that you are my slave, and know that you will feel the anger of a barbarian woman who has been wronged." So saying, she sent Rhode away. Rhode was in a hopeless plight: to tell Habrocomes she shrank from, out of love for Anthia, yet she was much afraid of the barbarian woman's anger.

She was very beautiful, Habrocomes, and plainly dressed; golden hair, charming eyes." While he was still speaking, Habrocomes cried out, "You have seen my Anthia, Hippothous! Where has she fled, then? What land holds her? Let us turn toward Cilicia, let us seek her; it is not far from the band.

So she prayed, and they went forward on the road. By now they had passed Coptos and were entering the borders of Ethiopia, when Hippothous fell upon them. He killed Psammis himself and many of those with him, took the goods, and made Anthia a captive.
She decided it would be best to confide first to Leucon what Manto had said. Now Rhode too had ties of love with Leucon, and they had been together even while in Ephesus.

Yes, by the very soul of Hyperanthes, do not willingly wrong me, but let us go where we can find Anthia." Hippothous promised to do everything, but said they must gather a few men for the safety of the road.

Gathering the captured goods, he led them to the cave appointed for the storing of their goods; there Anthia too was led. She did not recognize Hippothous, nor did Hippothous recognize Anthia. And whenever he asked her who she was and where she was from, she did not tell the truth, but said she was an Egyptian of the country, named Memphitis.

So then, taking him aside, she said, "Leucon, we are utterly undone; now we shall no longer have our companions. The daughter of our master Apsyrtus is in love with Habrocomes, a violent love, and threatens, if she does not get her way, to do us terrible harm.

So they were occupied with this, planning how they should go back to Cilicia. Meanwhile, for Anthia the thirty days had passed, and the preparations for the marriage were being made by Perilaus: victims were brought down from the country, and there was great abundance of everything besides. With him were his household and kinsmen, and many of the citizens too came to celebrate Anthia's wedding.

So consider what we must do; to contradict the barbarian woman is perilous, but to part Habrocomes from Anthia is impossible." Hearing this, Leucon was filled with tears, expecting great calamities from it; but at last he recovered and said, "Be silent, Rhode, for I will manage everything."

So Habrocomes seized his hair and tore his clothes, and said, "Alas for my misery! What has happened to me, wretch that I am? I, Habrocomes, until now so manly, who scorned Love, who reviled the god, am now taken and conquered, and forced to be the slave of a girl; and now someone appears more beautiful than I, and I call Love a god.

So saying, he went to Habrocomes. But he, in truth, had no other occupation than to love Anthia and be loved by her, to talk with her and listen to her talk. Coming to them, Leucon said, "What are we doing, companions? What are we planning, fellow slaves?

During the time when Anthia, taken from the band, had come to Tarsus, there arrived an old Ephesian, a physician by profession, Eudoxus by name; he had come to Egypt after falling into a shipwreck on his voyage.

So she was with Hippothous in the robbers' cave; meanwhile the governor of Egypt sent for Habrocomes, inquired into his story, learned the tale, pitied his fortune, gave him money, and promised to take him to Ephesus.
Polyidus did not think it enough to have overcome the robbers who had engaged him, but decided he must search out and clear Egypt, in case he might find Hippothous or any of his men.
O coward that I am in everything, and base! Will I not hold out now? Will I not remain noble? Will I not be more beautiful than Love?

You seem beautiful, Habrocomes, to one of our masters. Apsyrtus' daughter is in a sorry state over you, and to contradict a barbarian maiden in love is dangerous. So take counsel as you think best, save us all, and do not overlook us as we fall under our masters' anger."

This Eudoxus went about to the other men too, all those of Tarsus most esteemed, asking from some clothing, from others money, and telling each his misfortune; and he came to Perilaus too and said that he was an Ephesian and a physician by profession.

He gave the governor every thanks for his deliverance, but begged to be allowed to search for Anthia. And taking many gifts, he boarded a boat and set sail toward Italy, thinking to learn something there about Anthia. The governor of Egypt, learning the truth about Araxus, sent for Cyno and crucified her.

But on the second day the wind dropped, there was a calm, the voyage was slow, the sailors grew idle, and there was drinking and drunkenness—and the beginning of the prophecies.

The goatherd told him both her name—that it was Anthia—and the marriage, and the reverence he had shown her, and Moeris' love, and the order given against her, and the journey to Cilicia; and he said that the girl was always speaking of one Habrocomes. But Habrocomes did not tell him who he was, and rising at dawn he set off toward Cilicia, hoping to find Anthia there.

This Araxus had a wife loathsome to look upon, much worse to hear, surpassing all in licentiousness, Cyno by name. This Cyno fell in love with Habrocomes as soon as he was brought into the house, and could no longer restrain herself; she was terrible both in falling in love and in wishing to gratify her desire.

The next day Anthia came again to the temple with Hippothous, since there was no sailing for them, and sitting down by the offerings she wept and groaned. Meanwhile Leucon and Rhode came in, having left Habrocomes within, despondent over the same things; and coming they saw Anthia, and she was still unknown to them, but they put everything together at once—the tears, the offerings, the names, the appearance.

Meanwhile a woman appeared to Habrocomes, terrible to look upon, greater than human in size, wearing a crimson robe. Standing over the ship, she seemed to set it on fire, and the others perished, but he, with Anthia, swam to safety. As soon as he saw this he was troubled, and expected some calamity from the dream; and the calamity came to pass.

Araxus was fond of Habrocomes and treated him as a son; but Cyno made a proposal of intercourse, begged him to consent, promised that he would have her for a wife, and that she would kill Araxus. This seemed dreadful to Habrocomes, and he considered many things at once—Anthia, his oaths, the chastity he had so often wronged already; at last, as Cyno pressed him, he consented.
So little by little they recognized her; and falling at her knees they lay speechless. She marvelled who they were and what they wished, for she could never have hoped for Leucon and Rhode.

And when night came, she, thinking to have Habrocomes for a husband, killed Araxus and told Habrocomes what she had done. But he, unable to bear the woman's wantonness, left the house and abandoned her, saying that he would never lie beside a murderess.

They, coming to themselves, said, "Mistress Anthia, we are your servants, Leucon and Rhode, who shared your journey abroad and the robber band. But what fortune brings you here? Take heart, mistress; Habrocomes is safe and is here, always lamenting you."

When she came to herself, at daybreak she went to where the crowd of the people of Pelusium was, lamented her husband, and said that the newly bought slave had killed him; and she made much lamentation and seemed to speak credibly to the crowd. They at once seized Habrocomes, and binding him sent him up to the man who was then governor of Egypt.
Hearing this, Anthia was struck dumb at the words, but recovering with difficulty and recognizing them, she embraced and kissed them, and learned most clearly all about Habrocomes.

There happened to be at Rhodes pirates lying in wait for them, Phoenicians by race, in a great trireme. They lay at anchor as men carrying cargo, and they were many and bold. These had learned that on the ship there was gold and silver and many slaves of great value.
Hippothous the robber and his band stayed that night feasting, and on the next day set about the sacrifice. Everything was made ready—images of Ares, sacred boughs, garlands;

The whole crowd of the Rhodians flowed together, learning of the finding of Anthia and Habrocomes; and Hippothous was present too, and was recognized by Leucon and his companions, and himself learned who they were. Everything among them was happily settled, except that Habrocomes did not yet know these things; and they ran as they were to the house.
So they resolved to fall upon them, kill those who resisted, and carry off the rest to Phoenicia to be sold, along with the goods; for they despised them as no match in a fight.

and the sacrifice had to be performed in the customary manner. The victim that was to be sacrificed, whether man or beast, they hung from a tree and, standing apart, hurled javelins at it; and as many as hit the mark, the god seemed to accept their sacrifice; but as many as missed, they tried again to propitiate him. Anthia was to be offered in this way.

When Habrocomes heard from one of the Rhodians of the finding of Anthia, he ran through the middle of the city crying "Anthia!" like a madman. And so he met Anthia and her company near the temple of Isis, and a great crowd of the Rhodians followed.
The leader of the pirates was called Corymbus, a young man great to look upon, terrible in his gaze; his hair was unkempt and hung loose.

When all was ready and they wished to hang the girl up, a noise was heard in the wood and the tramp of men. It was the man set over the keeping of the peace in Cilicia, Perilaus by name, one of the foremost in power in Cilicia.

When they saw each other, they at once recognized each other; for this is what their souls wished. And embracing one another they sank to the ground; many emotions held them at once—pleasure, grief, fear, the memory of former things, the dread of what was to come. And the people of the Rhodians shouted blessings and cried out, calling Isis a great goddess and saying again, "We see Habrocomes and Anthia, the beautiful pair."

When the pirates had laid these plans, at first they sailed quietly alongside Habrocomes and his company; but at last—it was about midday, and all those on the ship were lying about from drink and idleness, some asleep, some listless—Corymbus and his men bore down upon them, driving their ship with great speed.
This Perilaus came upon the robbers with a great force and killed them all, taking only a few alive; only Hippothous managed to escape, snatching up his arms.

They, recovering themselves, rose and went into the temple of Isis, saying, "To you, greatest goddess, we owe thanks for our deliverance; through you, most honoured of all by us, we have recovered each other." And they rolled before the precinct and fell down at the altar. Then they were led to Leucon's house, and Hippothous moved his belongings to Leucon's; and they were ready for the voyage to Ephesus. When they had sacrificed that day and feasted, there were many and varied stories from all—what each had suffered and what each had done—and they prolonged the banquet far on, rejoicing to have recovered each other after so long.

When they came near, they leaped armed onto the ship, with their swords drawn. At that some flung themselves into the sea in terror and perished, while others, wishing to defend themselves, were cut down.

Perilaus took Anthia, and learning of the calamity that had threatened her, pitied her; but this pity for Anthia was the beginning of a great calamity. He led her, and the captured robbers, to Tarsus in Cilicia.

When night had come, they all rested as they could—Leucon and Rhode, Hippothous and the youth from Sicily who had followed him when he went to Italy, the handsome Cleisthenes; and Anthia rested with Habrocomes.

But Habrocomes and Anthia ran to Corymbus the pirate, and grasping his knees said, "Master, take the goods, and us too as your slaves, but spare our lives and kill no more of those who have willingly put themselves into your hands. By the sea itself, by your own right hand, lead us wherever you wish, and sell us as your slaves; only take pity on us, and put us under one master."

His daily sight of the girl led him into love, and little by little Perilaus was captured by Anthia. When they reached Tarsus, he handed the robbers over to prison, but tended Anthia. Perilaus had neither wife nor children, and no small store of wealth.
So he said to Anthia that she would be everything to Perilaus—wife and mistress and children.

At first she resisted, but having no idea what to do against a man who pressed her hard and urged her much, and fearing that he might attempt something more violent, she consented to the marriage, but begged him to wait a little while—thirty days—and to keep her untouched; and she pretended a reason. Perilaus was persuaded, and swore to keep her pure of marriage until the time had passed.

Hearing this, Corymbus at once ordered them to stop killing. He transferred the more valuable of the cargo, together with Habrocomes and Anthia and a few of the other servants, and set fire to the ship; all the rest were burned up, for he could neither carry them all off nor saw it safe to do so.

So she was in Tarsus with Perilaus, awaiting the time of the marriage; and Habrocomes was going along the road toward Cilicia. Not far from the robbers' cave (for he too had wandered from the direct road) he met Hippothous in arms.

When all the others had gone to sleep and there was deep quiet, Anthia embraced Habrocomes and wept, saying, "Husband and master, I have recovered you, after wandering over much land and sea, after escaping the threats of robbers and the plots of pirates and the outrages of brothel-keepers and bonds and pits and timbers and drugs and tombs.
It was a pitiable spectacle: some being carried off in the trireme, others, in the burning ship, stretching out their hands and lamenting.

Seeing him, Hippothous ran up, greeted him kindly, and asked him to be his companion on the road. "For I see, young man, whoever you are, that you are both beautiful to look upon and otherwise manly; and your wandering shows you to be one wholly wronged.

But I have come to you, Habrocomes, master of my soul, such as I was when I first left you for Syria from Tyre. No one persuaded me to sin—not Moeris in Syria, not Perilaus in Cilicia, not Psammis and Polyidus in Egypt, not Anchialus in Ethiopia, not my master at Tarentum—but I remain pure for you, having used every device of chastity.

Some cried, "Where will you be taken, masters? What land will receive you, and what city will you live in?" Others said, "O blessed are you, who are about to die happily before you have known bonds, before you have seen the slavery of pirates." So they spoke, while some were carried off and others burned.
So let us leave Cilicia and go to Cappadocia and the Pontus there; for they say that prosperous men live there."
But have you, Habrocomes, remained chaste, or has some other beautiful woman outshone me? Or has anyone compelled you to forget your oaths and me?"

Meanwhile the tutor of Habrocomes, an old man now, venerable to look upon and pitiable for his age, unable to bear to see Habrocomes carried off, threw himself into the sea and swam as if to overtake the trireme, saying, "To whom do you leave me, child—the old man, your guardian?

Habrocomes did not tell of his search for Anthia, but consented to Hippothous' urging, and they swore to work together and aid one another; for Habrocomes hoped, in his long wandering, to find Anthia.

So she spoke, and kissed him continually; and Habrocomes said, "I swear to you by this day we have at last found and longed for, that no maiden seemed beautiful to me, nor did any other woman I saw please me, but you have recovered Habrocomes such as you left him in Tyre in prison."

Where are you going, Habrocomes? Kill me yourself, unhappy as I am, and bury me; for what is life to me without you?" So he spoke, and at last, despairing of ever seeing Habrocomes again, he gave himself to the waves and died.

This of all things was the most pitiable to Habrocomes; he stretched out his hands to the old man and begged the pirates to take him up. But they paid him no heed, and after completing their voyage in three days they put in at Tyre, a city of Phoenicia, where the pirates had their home.

They did not bring them into the city itself, but to a nearby estate belonging to a man who was chief of a band of brigands, Apsyrtus by name, whose servant Corymbus was, for hire and a share of the spoils. During the passage of the voyage, from seeing him so much each day, Corymbus fell in love with Habrocomes, a violent love, and his familiarity with the youth inflamed him all the more.

During the voyage it seemed impossible to win him over, for he saw how wretchedly he was disposed from despondency, and he saw too that he was in love with Anthia; and to force him seemed dangerous, for he feared the youth might do himself some harm.

So all night long they made their defence to one another, and easily persuaded each other, since this was what they wished. When day came, they boarded a ship, put all their goods aboard, and set sail, escorted by the whole crowd of the Rhodians; and Hippothous went along with them too, bringing all his goods and Cleisthenes. After completing the voyage in a few days they put in at Ephesus.
But when they had put in at Tyre, Corymbus could endure it no longer. At first he tended Habrocomes, urged him to take heart, and showed him every care;

The whole city had already learned of their deliverance; and as they disembarked, they went at once, just as they were, to the temple of Artemis, and prayed much, and after sacrificing dedicated, among other offerings, a written account dedicated to the goddess of all that they had suffered and all they had done.

and Habrocomes thought that Corymbus took such care of him out of pity. Then Corymbus confided his love to one of his fellow pirates, Euxinus by name, and begged him to be his helper and to advise him by what means he might win the youth over.

And having done this, they went up into the city and built large tombs for their parents (who happened to have died before of old age and despondency), and they themselves lived the rest of their lives keeping their life together as a festival.

Euxinus heard Corymbus' tale with pleasure, for he himself was wretchedly disposed toward Anthia and loved the girl with a violent love. He told Corymbus his own case as well, and advised him not to torment himself any longer but to get to work;

And Leucon and Rhode shared everything with their foster-companions; and Hippothous too decided to live out the rest of his time in Ephesus. He raised a great tomb for Hyperanthes, returning to Lesbos to do so, and adopting Cleisthenes as his son, Hippothous lived in Ephesus with Habrocomes and Anthia.
Here ends Xenophon's Ephesian Tale of Anthia and Habrocomes.

for it was, he said, very ignoble that, after running such risks and venturing so much, they should not enjoy in safety what they had won by their labours. "We shall be able," he said, "to receive them as a special gift from Apsyrtus."

By saying this he easily persuaded the man, who was in love. And so they agreed in like manner to make their pleas, each on the other's behalf, and to win over—Euxinus, Habrocomes, and Corymbus, Anthia.
Meanwhile the two lay dejected, expecting much, talking with one another, and constantly swearing to keep the agreements they had made.

Then Corymbus and Euxinus came to them and, saying that they wished to speak privately, led them apart by themselves—the one Anthia, the other Habrocomes. The souls of the pair trembled, and they suspected nothing good.

So Euxinus spoke to Habrocomes on Corymbus' behalf: "Young man, it is natural that you should bear your misfortune hard, having become a slave instead of a free man, and poor instead of prosperous. But you must reckon everything to fortune, and be content with the spirit that governs you, and love the masters you have come to.

For know that it is possible for you to recover both prosperity and freedom, if you are willing to obey your master Corymbus; for he loves you with a violent love, and is ready to make you master of all that is his. You will suffer no hardship by yielding, but will make your master more kindly disposed toward you.

Consider the state you are in: no helper, this a foreign land, your masters pirates, and no escape from punishment for anyone who scorns Corymbus. What need have you now of a wife and such concerns? What need of a beloved, at your age? Cast everything aside; you must look to your master alone, and obey when he commands."

Hearing this, Habrocomes at once was speechless and could find no answer; he wept and groaned, looking inward at the state into which he had come. And then he said to Euxinus, "Allow me, master, to deliberate a little, and I will answer you on everything you have said."

So Euxinus withdrew; and Corymbus had spoken to Anthia of Euxinus' love, the present necessity, and the need for her by all means to obey her masters. He promised much—a lawful marriage, money, and abundance, if she would yield. She gave him a like answer, asking for a little time to deliberate.
